thai_name: ข้าวซอยไก่
description: Northern Thai coconut curry noodle soup with soft egg noodles, topped with crispy fried noodles.
how_to_eat: Add lime, pickled mustard greens and shallots from the side plate, then chilli oil to taste.
story: Chiang Mai's signature dish, linked to Chinese-Muslim (Haw) caravan traders who travelled through the north.

thai_name: ขนมจีนน้ำเงี้ยว
description: Fresh rice noodles in a tangy tomato-pork broth.
how_to_eat: Top with crispy garlic, bean sprouts and cabbage from the side, plus a squeeze of lime.
story: Named after the Ngiao (Shan) people, it reflects the Shan influence on Lanna cooking.

description: Grilled pork sausage packed with lemongrass, kaffir lime, galangal and chilli.
how_to_eat: Eat with sticky rice, fresh cabbage and raw chillies or ginger on the side.
story: A market staple and a classic Chiang Mai souvenir that people take home to Bangkok.

thai_name: น้ำพริกหนุ่ม
description: Smoky dip of roasted young green chillies, shallots and garlic.
how_to_eat: Dip pork rinds (khaep mu), steamed vegetables or a ball of sticky rice into it.
story: "Noom" means young. The dish is named after the young chillies, and it's on every Lanna table.

description: Slow-cooked pork belly curry, rich and sweet-sour rather than spicy, with ginger and tamarind.
how_to_eat: Order with steamed or sticky rice. It's often better the day after it's made.
story: Burmese in origin, adopted into Lanna cuisine. It's a festival and temple-fair favourite.

english_name: Khao Kha Moo (stewed pork leg rice)
description: Tender pork leg braised in soy and five-spice, served on rice with a boiled egg.
how_to_eat: Bite a raw garlic clove or chilli between mouthfuls, and use the sour chilli sauce.
story: Thai-Chinese comfort food. The cowboy-hat lady at Chang Phuak Gate made it famous in Chiang Mai.

thai_name: ผัดกะเพราหมูสับ
description: Minced pork stir-fried with holy basil, garlic and chilli, over rice.
how_to_eat: Add a fried egg (khai dao). Almost every Thai person does.
story: Thailand's go-to "I don't know what to eat" dish. Ask for it anywhere.

description: Pounded green papaya salad: sour, sweet, salty and hot.
how_to_eat: Share it with sticky rice and grilled chicken (gai yang).
story: From Isan (the northeast). Vendors pound each order fresh, so you can set your chilli count.

thai_name: ข้าวเหนียวมะม่วง
description: Sweet sticky rice with coconut cream and ripe mango.
how_to_eat: Eat it at room temperature, and pour the extra coconut cream over it.
story: It's best in the hot season (around March to May), when mangoes are at their peak.

description: Strong orange-hued black tea with sweetened condensed milk over ice.
how_to_eat: Say "wǎan nói" (หวานน้อย) if you want it less sweet.
story: Found at nearly every street stall. The bright orange colour comes from the tea blend.

description: Stir-fried thin rice noodles with egg, tofu, bean sprouts and a sweet-sour tamarind sauce.
how_to_eat: Season it yourself with the lime, crushed peanuts, sugar and chilli flakes on the table.
story: Promoted as a national dish in the mid-20th century, it is now Thailand's best-known noodle dish abroad.

description: Hot and sour soup with prawns, lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime leaves and lime juice.
how_to_eat: Eat it with rice and don't chew the lemongrass, galangal or lime leaves, they are there for flavour.
story: One of Thailand's most famous soups; ask for 'nám khôn' for the creamy version or 'nám săi' for the clear one.

description: Mild, creamy coconut milk soup with chicken, galangal, lemongrass and mushrooms.
how_to_eat: Spoon it over rice; the galangal slices are for flavour, not for eating.
story: 'Khàa' means galangal, the ginger-like root that gives the soup its name.

thai_name: แกงเขียวหวาน
description: Coconut green curry with Thai eggplant, basil and chicken, pork or beef.
how_to_eat: Pour it over rice, or eat it with fresh rice noodles (khanom jeen).
story: The name means 'sweet green curry', from the colour of the fresh green chillies in the paste.

description: Coconut curry made with red chilli paste, usually with pork, chicken or duck and bamboo shoots.
how_to_eat: Eat it with plain rice, which balances the richness.
story: A central Thai staple; the red version with roast duck (gaeng phet bpet) is a popular variation.

thai_name: แกงมัสมั่น
description: Mild, rich curry with warm spices, potatoes, peanuts and slow-cooked chicken or beef.
how_to_eat: Eat it with rice or roti; it is a good choice if you don't like much heat.
story: Its dried spices show the Persian and Muslim trading influences on Thai cooking.

description: Thick, slightly sweet red curry with peanuts, kaffir lime leaves and meat.
how_to_eat: Eat it with rice; the sauce is thick, so a little goes a long way.
story: Drier and richer than most Thai curries, it is often topped with a swirl of coconut cream.

thai_name: ข้าวมันไก่
description: Poached chicken on rice cooked in chicken fat and stock, with a clear soup and ginger-soy sauce.
how_to_eat: Dip each bite of chicken in the ginger and fermented soybean sauce; the soup comes free on the side.
story: Brought by Hainanese Chinese immigrants, it is now a Thai lunchtime classic.

description: Fried rice with egg, onion and your choice of chicken, pork, prawn or crab.
how_to_eat: Squeeze the lime wedge over it and add prik nam pla (fish sauce with chilli) to taste.
story: A safe everyday dish found everywhere; say 'khâao phàt gài' for chicken or 'gûng' for prawn.

description: Wide rice noodles stir-fried with dark soy sauce, egg, Chinese kale and meat.
how_to_eat: Add chilli vinegar and sugar from the condiment tray if you want more kick.
story: A Chinese-Thai wok dish; the slightly charred, smoky noodles are the sign of a good one.

description: Wide rice noodles topped with a thick, savoury gravy, Chinese kale and meat.
how_to_eat: Add chilli vinegar to cut through the gravy; you can ask for crispy egg noodles (mìi gròp) instead.
story: 'Râat nâa' means 'poured on top', describing the gravy ladled over the noodles.

description: Spicy stir-fried wide noodles with holy basil, chilli, garlic and meat.
how_to_eat: Ask for 'phèt nít nòi' (a little spicy) if you are careful with heat.
story: 'Khîi mao' means 'drunkard'; one story is that it was cooked as a late-night dish after drinking.

thai_name: ก๋วยเตี๋ยวน้ำ
description: Rice noodles in clear broth with pork, meatballs, bean sprouts and herbs.
how_to_eat: Choose the noodle size (sên lék thin, sên yài wide) and season with the four condiments: sugar, fish sauce, chilli flakes and vinegar.
story: Thailand's everyday street food, originally brought by Chinese immigrants.

thai_name: ก๋วยเตี๋ยวเรือ
description: Small bowls of rich, dark noodle soup with pork or beef, herbs and spices.
how_to_eat: Bowls are small, so people order several; stack the empty bowls to count the bill.
story: Once sold from boats on Bangkok's canals, which is why the bowls are small.

thai_name: บะหมี่หมูแดง
description: Yellow egg noodles with Chinese-style red roast pork and wontons, dry or in soup.
how_to_eat: Say 'hâeng' for dry noodles or 'náam' for soup.
story: A Chinese-Thai classic, often sold at the same stall as rice with red pork.

thai_name: ข้าวหมูแดง
description: Sliced Chinese-style red roast pork on rice with a sweet, thick red gravy and a boiled egg.
how_to_eat: Add the sliced chillies in soy sauce on the side for contrast.
story: A Teochew Chinese dish that became a Thai lunchtime staple.

thai_name: ข้าวหมูกรอบ
description: Crispy pork belly on rice with sweet gravy, often served with red pork.
how_to_eat: Dip the pork in the chilli soy sauce served on the side.
story: Often sold at the same stall as rice with red pork; order both as 'khâao mŭu daeng mŭu gròp'.

description: Smooth, thick rice porridge with pork balls, ginger and often an egg.
how_to_eat: Stir in the egg, then add pepper and fried garlic; it is a common breakfast.
story: A Chinese-style congee eaten across Thailand, especially in the morning.

description: Rice in a light clear broth with pork, prawns or fish, garlic oil and celery.
how_to_eat: Add pepper and a little fish sauce; it is a popular breakfast and late-night meal.
story: Unlike jok, the rice grains stay whole in a clear soup.

description: Sweet, garlicky marinated pork grilled on skewers over charcoal.
how_to_eat: Eat it with a small bag of sticky rice as a grab-and-go breakfast.
story: A morning street-food staple; buy a few skewers and a bag of sticky rice.

description: Charcoal-grilled marinated chicken with a sweet or spicy dipping sauce.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and som tam, tearing the chicken with your fingers.
story: Strongly linked to Isan (the northeast), where it is eaten with sticky rice and papaya salad.

description: Minced meat tossed with lime, fish sauce, chilli, toasted rice powder and fresh herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and raw vegetables like cabbage and long beans.
story: The Isan (northeastern) version is sour and spicy; the Northern version, laab mueang, is quite different.

description: Sliced grilled pork tossed with lime, chilli, toasted rice powder and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and fresh vegetables.
story: 'Náam tòk' means 'waterfall', often said to refer to the meat juices dripping as it grills.

description: Thin slices of boiled pork covered in a sharp lime, garlic and chilli sauce.
how_to_eat: Eat it as a shared dish with drinks or rice; the raw garlic and chilli are strong.
story: A popular drinking snack (gàp glâem) at Thai restaurants and bars.

thai_name: ยำวุ้นเส้น
description: Glass noodles tossed with minced pork, prawns, lime, chilli, onion and herbs.
how_to_eat: Share it as a side dish with rice.
story: 'Yam' is the Thai family of sour, spicy, salad-like dishes.

description: Whole fish packed with lemongrass, crusted in salt and grilled over charcoal.
how_to_eat: Peel off the salty skin and wrap the fish with noodles and vegetables in lettuce, dipped in seafood sauce.
story: A night-market favourite; the salt crust keeps the fish moist.

thai_name: ปลากะพงนึ่งมะนาว
description: Whole sea bass steamed in a sour, spicy lime, garlic and chilli broth.
how_to_eat: Share the fish from the middle of the table and spoon the broth over rice.
story: Often served in a fish-shaped pot kept hot with a flame at the table.

description: Deep-fried fish cakes with red curry paste, long beans and kaffir lime leaves.
how_to_eat: Dip them in the sweet cucumber relish served on the side.
story: A common starter and street snack.

thai_name: ปอเปี๊ยะทอด
description: Crispy fried rolls filled with glass noodles, vegetables and sometimes pork.
how_to_eat: Dip them in sweet chilli sauce.
story: A Chinese-origin snack found at markets across Thailand.

description: Grilled turmeric-marinated pork or chicken skewers with peanut sauce.
how_to_eat: Dip in peanut sauce and eat with the cucumber relish and toasted bread.
story: Came to Thailand from the Malay world in the south.

description: Puffy, crispy deep-fried omelette, plain or with minced pork.
how_to_eat: Eat it on rice with sriracha or chilli fish sauce.
story: A cheap comfort food that almost every Thai person grows up eating.

description: Egg fried in hot oil until the edges are crispy.
how_to_eat: Add one on top of pad kra pao or fried rice by saying 'sài khài daao'.
story: 'Khài daao' means 'star egg', from its shape.

thai_name: ผัดผักบุ้ง
description: Morning glory greens flash-fried with garlic, chilli and soybean sauce.
how_to_eat: Order it as a shared vegetable side with rice.
story: Cooked over very high heat; at some places the flames rise dramatically from the wok.

description: Mixed vegetables stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce.
how_to_eat: A good vegetarian-friendly side; say 'mâi sài núea sàt' for no meat.
story: A standard dish at every made-to-order (aahăan taam sàng) shop.

thai_name: ไก่ผัดเม็ดมะม่วงหิมพานต์
description: Stir-fried chicken with cashews, onion, dried chillies and a sweet savoury sauce.
how_to_eat: Eat it with rice; the dried chillies are mostly for aroma.
story: A Chinese-influenced stir-fry that is very popular with visitors.

thai_name: ผัดเปรี้ยวหวาน
description: Stir-fried meat with pineapple, tomato, cucumber and onion in a sweet-sour sauce.
how_to_eat: Eat it with rice; good for kids and anyone avoiding heat.
story: A Chinese-Thai dish found at most made-to-order shops.

thai_name: ข้าวคลุกกะปิ
description: Rice fried with shrimp paste, served with sweet pork, egg, green mango and shallots.
how_to_eat: Mix all the toppings into the rice before eating.
story: A central Thai dish that balances salty, sweet and sour in one plate.

description: Rolled rice noodles in a peppery broth with crispy pork, pork offal and egg.
how_to_eat: Ask for 'mâi ao khrûeang nai' if you don't want offal.
story: A Teochew Chinese noodle soup; the noodles curl into little tubes as they cook.

description: Noodle soup in a pink broth coloured with fermented red bean curd, with fish balls and squid.
how_to_eat: Season with the table condiments; it tastes slightly sweet.
story: Its bright pink colour makes it easy to spot on a menu photo.

thai_name: ขนมจีนน้ำยา
english_name: Khanom Jeen Nam Ya (rice noodles with fish curry)
description: Fresh fermented rice noodles with a fish and coconut curry sauce.
how_to_eat: Help yourself to the free fresh vegetables and herbs, and add them on top.
story: Khanom jeen is one of Thailand's oldest noodles, made from fermented rice.

description: Thin, sour tamarind curry with fish or prawns and vegetables, without coconut milk.
how_to_eat: Spoon it over rice; it is sour and spicy, not creamy.
story: A central and southern Thai curry; the southern version (gaeng lueang) is yellow and fiery.

thai_name: แกงจืดเต้าหู้หมูสับ
english_name: Clear Soup with Tofu and Pork
description: Mild clear soup with soft tofu, minced pork, glass noodles and vegetables.
how_to_eat: Order it to share alongside spicy dishes; it cools the palate.
story: 'Jùet' means 'bland': it is the gentle soup on a Thai table.

english_name: Tom Saep (Isan hot and sour soup)
description: Spicy, sour clear soup with pork ribs or beef, lemongrass, galangal and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice; it is spicier and more herbal than tom yum.
story: 'Sâep' is the Isan word for 'delicious' and spicy.

description: Cook-it-yourself meal: grill meat on a domed pan while soup cooks vegetables around the edge.
how_to_eat: Rub pork fat on the dome first, grill on top, and let the juices run into the soup below.
story: A hugely popular social meal, usually buffet-style, eaten with friends and beer.

description: Glass noodles, egg, meat and vegetables in broth, served as soup (náam) or dry-fried (hâeng).
how_to_eat: Mix in the red, chilli-garlic suki sauce to taste.
story: A Thai take on Japanese sukiyaki, very different from the original.

description: Crispy fried batter with egg and mussels or oysters, on bean sprouts.
how_to_eat: Dip it in sriracha sauce.
story: A Chinese-Thai street-food favourite cooked on a big flat griddle.

thai_name: กุ้งอบวุ้นเส้น
description: Prawns baked in a clay pot on glass noodles with ginger, pepper and soy.
how_to_eat: Mix the noodles well; they soak up all the prawn juices.
story: A Chinese-Thai seafood dish served in its clay pot.

thai_name: ปลาหมึกย่าง
description: Squid grilled on skewers with a spicy green seafood dipping sauce.
how_to_eat: Dip it in the green nám jîm sii-fúut; it is very spicy.
story: A common night-market and beach snack.

thai_name: ไส้กรอกอีสาน
description: Slightly sour fermented pork and rice sausage, grilled in little balls or links.
how_to_eat: Eat it with fresh ginger, raw chilli and cabbage in the same bite.
story: The sourness comes from fermentation, a traditional northeastern way to preserve meat.

description: Juicy, marinated pork neck grilled and sliced, with a spicy jaew dipping sauce.
how_to_eat: Dip each slice in the jaew (chilli and toasted rice sauce) and eat it with sticky rice.
story: An Isan-style grill favourite, often ordered with drinks.

description: Crispy fried chicken, often topped with fried garlic or shallots.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and sweet chilli sauce.
story: Thai street-style fried chicken; Hat Yai in the south is famous for its version.

description: Pan-fried flatbread, often with banana and egg, topped with condensed milk and sugar.
how_to_eat: Order 'roo-tii glûay khài' for banana and egg.
story: Brought by South Asian and Muslim communities; in Thailand it is mostly eaten as a sweet snack.

description: Small half-moon coconut rice pancakes, crispy outside and custardy inside.
how_to_eat: Eat them hot straight from the pan.
story: 'Khrók' is the mortar the cast-iron pan resembles.

english_name: Bua Loy (rice balls in coconut milk)
description: Small chewy rice flour balls in warm, sweet coconut milk.
how_to_eat: Ask for a sweet egg on top with 'bua loi khài wăan'.
story: 'Bua loi' means 'floating lotus', from the way the balls float.

thai_name: ทับทิมกรอบ
description: Crunchy water chestnut cubes in red jelly coating, served with coconut milk and ice.
how_to_eat: Stir everything together so each spoon has coconut milk and ice.
story: 'Tháp-thim' means ruby, from their red colour.

thai_name: กล้วยบวชชี
description: Banana pieces simmered in sweet, slightly salty coconut milk.
how_to_eat: It is served warm; a good dessert after spicy food.
story: The name means 'bananas ordained as nuns', from the white coconut milk.

description: Strong black tea with lime and sugar over ice.
how_to_eat: Say 'wăan nói' for less sweet.
story: A refreshing alternative to milky cha yen, sold at the same stalls.

description: Strong black iced coffee brewed with roasted grains and sweetened.
how_to_eat: Say 'mâi sài nám dtaan' for no sugar.
story: A traditional Chinese-Thai coffee shop drink, older than the modern café scene.

thai_name: น้ำมะพร้าว
description: Fresh coconut water, often served in the whole young coconut.
how_to_eat: Scrape out the soft flesh with a spoon after drinking.
story: Young coconuts are sold chilled at markets and fruit stalls.

thai_name: ผัดวุ้นเส้น
description: Glass noodles stir-fried with egg, vegetables and meat or prawns.
how_to_eat: Add chilli fish sauce if you want more flavour.
story: A light made-to-order dish, less oily than most noodle stir-fries.

description: Chicken stir-fried with fresh ginger, mushrooms, onion and soy sauce.
how_to_eat: Eat it with rice; the ginger gives warmth rather than heat.
story: A mild Chinese-Thai stir-fry.

thai_name: ปลาราดพริก
description: Whole deep-fried fish covered in a sweet, sour and spicy chilli sauce.
how_to_eat: Share it at the table; eat the crispy fins too.
story: 'Râat phrík' means 'topped with chilli'.

thai_name: หมูทอดกระเทียม
description: Pork fried with lots of garlic and pepper, served on rice.
how_to_eat: Add a fried egg and chilli fish sauce.
story: A mild made-to-order favourite, good for anyone avoiding chilli.

description: Fiery, herbal curry without coconut milk, with meat, vegetables and krachai root.
how_to_eat: Eat it with plenty of rice; it is one of the spiciest curries.
story: 'Bpàa' means forest: a country-style curry made without coconut.

description: Mixed seafood tossed with lime, chilli, onion, celery and herbs.
how_to_eat: Share it as a side with rice or drinks.
story: A 'yam' salad; the dressing is sour, salty, sweet and spicy.

thai_name: น้ำพริกอ่อง
description: Mild, chunky dip of minced pork, tomato and chilli paste, a bit like a Thai bolognese.
how_to_eat: Scoop it with pork crackling (khaep moo), raw or boiled vegetables and sticky rice.
story: One of the best-known Northern chilli dips, often served next to nam prik noom.

description: Minced meat with a dry spice mix of dried chillies, long pepper and other spices, often with blood or offal.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and bitter fresh herbs; ask 'sùk' for fully cooked, since some versions are raw.
story: Unlike the lime-sour Isan larb, the Northern version gets its flavour from a dry spice blend.

description: Northern larb that is stir-fried in the pan until cooked, with spices and herbs.
how_to_eat: A cooked, safer choice than raw laab; eat it with sticky rice and herbs.
story: 'Khûa' means dry-fried in a pan.

description: Clear, herbal Northern curry with many local vegetables and leaves, usually with chicken or frog.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice; the mix of vegetables changes by season.
story: A country-style curry without coconut milk, typical of Lanna home cooking.

description: Thin, spicy stewed curry, often with beef or pork and offal, flavoured with dill and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice; ask 'mâi sài khrûeang nai' if you don't want offal.
story: A slow-cooked Northern home dish without coconut milk.

description: Crunchy puffed pork rind, sometimes with a layer of fat attached.
how_to_eat: Use it to scoop up nam prik noom and nam prik ong.
story: A classic Chiang Mai snack and souvenir, sold in big bags at markets.

description: Tangy fermented pork sausage with garlic and chilli, eaten raw-fermented or fried.
how_to_eat: Eat it with fresh ginger, shallots, peanuts and chilli; or order 'nǎem thâwt' fried with egg.
story: Called jin som (จิ๊นส้ม) in Northern Thai; it is sour from fermentation, not vinegar.

description: Boiled young jackfruit pounded with chilli paste, pork and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and pork crackling.
story: Jackfruit (khà-nŭn) sounds like 'support', so it is often cooked for ceremonies and housewarmings.

description: Northern curry of young jackfruit with pork ribs, tomato and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice.
story: A traditional Lanna curry made without coconut milk.

thai_name: ข้าวกั๊นจิ๊น
description: Rice mixed with pork and pork blood, wrapped in banana leaf and steamed.
how_to_eat: Eat it with fried garlic, dried chilli, cucumber and spring onion on the side.
story: A Northern Thai and Shan dish; 'gán jín' means 'squeezed meat' in Northern Thai.

description: Sweet sticky rice with coconut milk and beans, roasted inside a bamboo tube.
how_to_eat: Peel the bamboo back in strips and eat the rice from the thin inner skin.
story: Roasting in bamboo is an old rural way of cooking rice while travelling.

description: Stir-fried mix of leftover curries with glass noodles, bamboo shoots and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice.
story: 'Hó' means 'mixed together': traditionally made from leftovers after festivals.

description: Shredded boiled chicken mixed with Northern chilli paste, herbs and chicken broth.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and fresh vegetables.
story: 'Jín' means 'meat' in Northern Thai.

thai_name: ข้าวเหนียว
description: Steamed glutinous rice, served in a small basket or bag and eaten by hand.
how_to_eat: Roll a small ball with your right hand and use it to scoop dips and meat.
story: The everyday staple of Northern and Northeastern Thailand, served in a woven kratip basket.

description: Sour soup of mustard greens with pork ribs, tamarind and fermented soybean.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and a Northern chilli dip.
story: A cool-season Lanna soup, made when mustard greens are flowering.

description: Northern curry of tender banana stem with chicken or pork and herbs.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice.
story: A thrifty Lanna dish that uses the soft inner banana trunk.

english_name: Aep Moo (pork grilled in banana leaf)
description: Minced pork with egg, chilli paste and herbs, wrapped in banana leaf and grilled.
how_to_eat: Unwrap it and eat with sticky rice.
story: 'Áep' is a Northern way of grilling food in a flat banana-leaf parcel.

thai_name: น้ำพริกตาแดง
english_name: Nam Prik Taa Daeng (red-eye chilli paste)
description: Dry, smoky red chilli paste of roasted dried chillies, garlic and shallots.
how_to_eat: Use it sparingly with sticky rice and vegetables; it is very hot.
story: A Northern pantry staple that keeps for a long time.

description: Smoky roasted long eggplant pounded with chilli, garlic, shallot and boiled egg.
how_to_eat: Eat it with sticky rice and pork crackling.
story: A simple Northern countryside dip.

thai_name: ห่อนึ่งไก่
english_name: Hor Nueng Gai (steamed chicken in banana leaf)
description: Chicken with Northern curry paste, herbs and vegetables, wrapped in banana leaf and steamed.
how_to_eat: Open the parcel and eat it with sticky rice.
story: 'Hàw nûeng' means 'wrapped and steamed'; it is common at Northern markets.

thai_name: ข้าวซอยเนื้อ
description: Northern coconut curry noodle soup with tender beef, topped with crispy noodles.
how_to_eat: Add lime, pickled mustard greens, shallots and chilli oil from the side.
story: Beef khao soi is common at the Chiang Mai shops with Chinese-Muslim (Haw) roots.

description: Fermented wild tea leaves, chewed with salt or ginger as a traditional snack.
how_to_eat: Chew it slowly like gum; it is mildly caffeinated.
story: The hill forests around Chiang Mai have grown tea for fermenting as miang for centuries.

description: Crispy fried sticky rice crackers drizzled with caramelised cane sugar.
how_to_eat: Buy a bag as a snack or souvenir.
story: A famous product of Lampang and other Northern provinces.

thai_name: แกงกระด้าง
description: Pork trotter curry that sets into a cold, savoury jelly.
how_to_eat: Eat it cold with sticky rice.
story: A cool-season Lanna dish: the jelly sets naturally in the cold weather.

description: Fermented soybeans pressed into dry discs or a paste, used to season Northern food.
how_to_eat: Look for it grilled as a snack or inside Northern curries and chilli dips.
story: A Shan and Northern Thai staple that gives many Lanna dishes their deep flavour.

description: Bottled drinking water, sold cold at almost every shop and stall.
how_to_eat: Ask for "náam yen" (น้ำเย็น) if you want it chilled. Many restaurants also give free jugs of filtered water.
story: Thais rarely drink tap water; sealed bottles or filtered water are the norm.

description: A glass filled with ice, to pour your water, soft drink or beer over.
how_to_eat: Order it alongside a bottle; the cylinder ice with a hole in the middle is factory-made and generally safe.
story: Beer on ice is completely normal in Thailand, because of the heat.

description: Coca-Cola, usually served in a glass bottle or can with a glass of ice.
how_to_eat: Say "khóhk" with a short, high tone; "Pepsi" (เป๊ปซี่) is just as common.
story: Street stalls often pour soft drinks into a plastic bag with ice and a straw for take-away.

thai_name: เบียร์ช้าง
description: A strong, popular Thai lager. Cháang means elephant.
how_to_eat: Usually drunk over ice. Alcohol is not sold in shops from 14:00 to 17:00 or after midnight.
story: The green elephant label is one of the best-known Thai brands.

thai_name: เบียร์สิงห์
description: A full-bodied Thai lager, Thailand's oldest beer brand.
how_to_eat: Say "sǐng", not "sing-ha". Often drunk over ice.
story: Brewed since 1933 by Boon Rawd, the first Thai brewery.

thai_name: เบียร์ลีโอ
description: A light, cheap and very popular Thai lager.
how_to_eat: Often ordered by the big bottle (ขวดใหญ่) to share, poured over ice.
story: Made by the same company as Singha; it has a leopard on the label.

description: Strong coffee with sweetened condensed and evaporated milk over ice.
how_to_eat: Very sweet by default; ask for "wǎan nói" (less sweet). For black, ask for "gaa-fae dam" (กาแฟดำ).
story: Chiang Mai is surrounded by coffee farms, so good local beans are easy to find.

description: Hot Thai-style coffee, usually with condensed milk.
how_to_eat: Ask for "mâi sài nom" (ไม่ใส่นม) for no milk.
story: Old-style coffee shops serve it with a small glass of hot tea as a chaser.

description: Thai tea with sugar over ice, without milk.
how_to_eat: A lighter option than milk tea; still sweet unless you ask for less.
story: The same orange tea as chaa yen, just without the milk.

description: Iced milk sweetened with red sala syrup, bright pink.
how_to_eat: Very sweet; a favourite with kids.
story: The pink colour comes from sala syrup, a sweet red flavouring.

thai_name: ชาเขียวเย็น
description: Sweet milky green tea over ice.
how_to_eat: Much sweeter than Japanese green tea; ask for less sweet if needed.
story: A Thai street-stall classic, usually bright green.

thai_name: น้ำส้มคั้น
description: Freshly squeezed Thai orange juice, sometimes with a pinch of salt.
how_to_eat: Sold in small bottles at markets; ask "mâi sài glueah" (ไม่ใส่เกลือ) for no salt.
story: Northern Thailand grows many oranges; the juice is often more yellow than orange.

description: Fruit blended with ice and sugar syrup; say the fruit first, e.g. น้ำมะม่วงปั่น (mango).
how_to_eat: Choose a fruit and ask for less sweet; some stalls add condensed milk.
story: Fruit-shake stalls are everywhere in Chiang Mai's old town and night markets.

description: Freshly pressed sugarcane juice, naturally sweet.
how_to_eat: Drink it fresh and cold; it is already sweet with no added sugar.
story: Often pressed on the spot at markets.

description: A sweet drink made from dried longan fruit, served over ice.
how_to_eat: Tastes a little smoky and caramel-like.
story: Longan is a famous crop of Chiang Mai and Lamphun.

description: A light, sweet lemongrass infusion served cold.
how_to_eat: Refreshing on hot days; less sweet than most Thai drinks.
story: Thais consider lemongrass good for digestion.

description: A sweet green drink made from pandan leaves, served cold.
how_to_eat: Has a light vanilla-like smell.
story: Pandan is also used to flavour many Thai desserts.
